Population & the Future · The Big Story

Japan is one decimal point from a number that changes everything.

Nearly three in ten people in Japan are 65 or older. But the number is only the first layer. The real surprise is what it is forcing the country to invent.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
October 7, 2026 · 9 min read

Walk into a Japanese convenience store early in the morning and the scene can look almost timeless: neatly arranged rice balls, the soft electronic greeting at the door, a delivery arriving exactly when expected. Look closer, though, and you can see a country quietly renegotiating who does the work, who needs help, and how a neighborhood keeps moving.

The figure published this week is 29.6%. That is the share of Japan’s population aged 65 or older, according to figures summarized by Nippon.com from government data. The total is about 36.2 million people. Among countries with populations above 40 million, Japan remains far ahead of the rest.

A decimal point can seem abstract. Yet 29.6% means Japan is now close enough to 30% that the old language of an “aging society” no longer captures the scale. This is not a distant forecast. It is the operating environment of the country today.

The tension behind an ordinary day

Japan still feels fast. Trains run, restaurants open, packages move overnight. That smoothness can hide the pressure underneath: fewer working-age people are supporting more older residents, regional services have fewer staff, and the number of people over 75 is rising particularly quickly.

The Statistics Bureau’s September population estimate put the 65-plus population at roughly 36.21 million. The population aged 15 to 64 fell by more than 220,000 from a year earlier, while the population aged 75 and over rose by nearly 480,000. The two lines are moving in opposite directions.

Here is the twist: the most important story is not that Japan has more older people. It is that Japan must redesign normal life before most other large countries do.

A crisis—and a live prototype

That redesign reaches far beyond nursing homes. Retailers experiment with easier packaging and smaller portions. Municipalities rethink transport for residents who no longer drive. Factories and logistics companies invest in automation because recruitment alone cannot fill every gap. Homes, stations and public information are being reconsidered for bodies that move, see and hear differently.

This does not make every solution a success, nor does technology erase the human cost of loneliness, care shortages or shrinking towns. But it does turn Japan into a live prototype. Italy, South Korea, China and many other countries are moving toward versions of the same challenge. They can watch what Japan tries—and what fails.

The part visitors may miss

For an overseas visitor, demographic change rarely arrives as a dramatic scene. It appears as a bus route with fewer departures, an unmanned checkout, a robot delivering food, a shopping street where shutters stay down, or a small-town festival sustained by people in their seventies.

It also appears in language. The phrase 少子高齢化 (shōshi kōreika) combines a declining number of children with an aging population. It is often translated as “the declining birthrate and aging population,” but in Japan it carries the weight of an issue discussed for decades without an easy answer.

What to watch next

Do not watch only the national percentage. Watch three places where the consequences become concrete: the number of workers entering health and elder care; the survival of transport, hospitals and schools outside major cities; and whether productivity gains improve people’s lives rather than simply covering missing labor.

Japan is one decimal point away from 30%. Crossing that line will not suddenly transform the country. The transformation is already happening—in the ordinary places that still look unchanged.
